Keywords: Coastal Salt Pans and Meat Brining
RagShortTexts: Salt revenues arise from particular production, market and transport rights.
A mature uniform later French gabelle administration is not assumed to exist in 1259.

Variants.Content: Salt is essential to cooking and preserving food, making its production, carriage and sale valuable sources of revenue. Rights over a saltworks, market or route may belong to different rulers, towns or other holders, and obligations vary widely. In 1259 there is no single mature French gabelle administration governing every household's purchase. A useful account identifies the particular toll, privilege or monopoly instead of importing later offices and penalties wholesale. Costs can fall differently on producers, carriers and buyers; a levy that enriches one treasury may encourage a competing route or make preserved food harder for poor families to afford.

Coastal salt pans, such as those at Chioggia for Venice or Hyeres in Provence, gave their owners dependable income. That income paid for war fleets and diplomatic bribes, so a lord who held a lagoon or saltworks could finance a campaign without waiting on his king. Control of salt was control of the purse.

Every household needs salt for cooking and preserving food, so control of its sale can sharpen a local dispute over tolls or monopoly. Charges and privileges differ between regions in 1259. The later French gabelle administration, with its familiar offices and penalties, must not be treated as a uniform institution already searching every peasant's house.
